introduction: Continuous integration runs your team's checks when code changes. Its value is not a green badge by itself: it makes the evidence repeatable and makes a failed requirement visible before release.
You will create a dedicated private Taskboard repository, run real lint and test jobs in GitLab, and submit an intentionally broken merge request. No cloud deployment credentials are needed.
prerequisites: Complete the local-release capstone and retain its source/evidence.
Use a GitLab account and private learning project with a Linux Docker runner available. Inspect runner availability and compute quota before the first pipeline.
The dedicated CI repository will live at ~/dev-opps-delivery. Keep .env, reports, venvs and course browsing files out of it.

For a zero-charge runner, use your own disposable local Ubuntu VM. The Learn without a cloud bill handbook explains how to perform only week 10's basic installation/register steps before week 9, with privileged mode off. Hosted runner minutes are optional; do not buy compute for this course.

concepts.title: A pipeline is code running somewhere
paragraphs: The .gitlab-ci.yml file describes jobs. GitLab schedules them; a runner executes their scripts in a configured environment. An image declaration only works with an executor that supports it. A pending job can mean no eligible runner, not broken application code.

Jobs have exit statuses. A failed required job must stop your release procedure. Publishing a JUnit report makes failures readable, but the report alone does not enforce a gate: the test command must return nonzero and the job must not ignore it.
concepts.example: Adding `|| true` after pytest would hide its failed exit status even though a report still contains failures.
concepts.judgment: Read both the job script and runner authority. Pipeline authors can execute code with whatever access the job receives.

concepts.title: Workflow rules choose which pipelines exist
paragraphs: A push to a branch with an open merge request can otherwise trigger both branch and merge-request pipelines. The workflow below allows merge-request pipelines, suppresses redundant branch pipelines for open MRs, and allows other branch pipelines.
Job stages organize execution, but workflow rules run before jobs are considered. Variables in these rules are supplied by GitLab; they are not values you should invent or store as secrets.
concepts.example: A new feature branch gets a branch pipeline. Once its MR is open, MR pipelines become the relevant change evidence.
concepts.judgment: Know why a pipeline was created or suppressed. More duplicate runs do not automatically mean better coverage.

concepts.title: A merge decision needs an enforced or explicit gate
paragraphs: In project settings, enable the merge check requiring successful pipelines where available, and protect main from direct unreviewed pushes. Confirm the rule with an actual failing MR rather than assuming a red icon blocks merging.

Some approval and protected-environment capabilities depend on the GitLab offering/tier. If a desired control is unavailable, document a manual release-owner check and its weaker enforcement instead of claiming a technical guarantee.
concepts.example: A maintainer who can change CI and bypass branch policy has more effective authority than a contributor whose MR only runs untrusted tests.
concepts.judgment: Make the control and its exceptions visible in the handoff.

steps.title: Create a repository containing only the application
steps.purpose: In GitLab create a blank private project named dev-opps-taskboard without initializing a README. Inspect Settings → CI/CD → Runners for an available Linux Docker runner and the relevant usage quota. In your terminal copy only the intended application inputs.

commands.code:
cd ~/dev-opps-lab/app/taskboard
test ! -e ~/dev-opps-delivery || { printf '%s\n' 'Destination already exists; inspect it before continuing.'; exit 1; }
mkdir ~/dev-opps-delivery || exit 1
cp -R reference starter migrations tests tools ci requirements.lock requirements-dev.lock Dockerfile compose.yaml pytest.ini .gitignore .dockerignore .env.example README.md ~/dev-opps-delivery/ || exit 1
cd ~/dev-opps-delivery
git init -b main
git config user.name 'Dev Opps Learner'
git config user.email 'learner@example.invalid'
git status --short
explain: test checks the new destination is absent; stop if it exists rather than overwriting it. mkdir creates this dedicated repository folder.
cp lists the exact required application files; it omits .env, .venv, reports and parent Git metadata.
git init creates a new main branch. Local author configuration applies only here. status lets you inspect the files before committing.
An explicit failure branch stops the sequence instead of letting later commands run after a failed prerequisite. Correct the cause and reopen Bash if the guard closed this terminal.
commands.expected: Only application source/configuration appears in the new repository; no credentials or generated data.
commands.troubleshoot: If a named file is missing, inspect the learner lab version. Do not replace this with an indiscriminate home-directory copy.

steps.checkpoint: Review .gitignore and the staged file list before sharing anything with GitLab.

steps.title: Write the complete initial pipeline
steps.purpose: This first pipeline has no image build or deployment authority. The lint job selects correctness-focused rules; it is not a claim that formatting or every possible static rule was checked.

commands.code:
cat > .gitlab-ci.yml <<'YAML'
stages: [check]
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"'
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS'
      when: never
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH'
default:
  image: python:3.14-slim-bookworm@sha256:48b13b003dda20b16f9442b8475aa05fe21bf6579a8c881db92ffb4d8fd20f83
lint:
  stage: check
  script:
    - python -m pip install --no-cache-dir ruff==0.11.13
    - python -m ruff check --target-version py312 --select E9,F63,F7,F82 reference starter tools
unit:
  stage: check
  script:
    - python -m pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements-dev.lock
    - python -m pytest tests/unit tests/contract --junitxml=reports/unit.xml
  artifacts:
    when: always
    expire_in: 14 days
    reports:
      junit: reports/unit.xml
YAML
git add reference starter migrations tests tools ci requirements.lock requirements-dev.lock Dockerfile compose.yaml pytest.ini .gitignore .dockerignore .env.example README.md .gitlab-ci.yml
git diff --cached --stat
git commit -m 'Add Taskboard with required lint and unit checks'
explain: The quoted YAML here-document preserves GitLab's $ variables literally.
stages defines check. workflow controls pipeline creation as explained above. default.image selects the pinned Python runtime for Docker-executor jobs.
lint installs a recorded Ruff version and checks syntax/undefined-name correctness rules with a Python 3.12 target. unit installs the locked test dependencies and runs real unit/adapter checks.
artifacts.when=always retains the JUnit report even after failure; expire_in bounds retention. git add stages only named inputs; diff --cached --stat reviews the list; commit records the pipeline.
commands.expected: One committed pipeline with two executable checks and finite report retention.
commands.troubleshoot: Before pushing, use GitLab's pipeline editor/CI lint validation for this YAML. A valid YAML document still needs GitLab-specific validation.

steps.checkpoint: Explain why a JUnit report cannot substitute for pytest's exit status.

steps.title: Connect the project and inspect the first run
steps.purpose: Copy the actual clone URL from your private project's Code menu. Authenticate through your configured Git credential/SSH workflow; do not embed a token in the URL or evidence.

commands.code:
read -r -p 'Paste your private GitLab project clone URL: ' GITLAB_REPO
git remote add origin "$GITLAB_REPO"
git push -u origin main
explain: read obtains your actual destination without a fabricated namespace. -r preserves literal backslashes; quotes keep the URL one argument.
remote add records the destination. push -u uploads main and establishes its upstream.
commands.expected: GitLab's Build → Pipelines shows a run for the recorded commit. Inspect lint and unit logs and the Tests report.
commands.troubleshoot: If pending, inspect eligible runner tags/executor and quota. If denied, fix project access through normal GitLab authentication without pasting secrets into the course.

steps.checkpoint: Enable the project's successful-pipeline merge check, protect main, and record the exact settings available in your tier.

failure.title: Submit a real validation defect
failure.boundary: Use a feature branch in the private learning repository. Never merge the broken version. The fault changes only the lower title-length boundary.

inject.code:
git switch -c practice/ci-empty-title || exit 1
python3 - <<'PY' || exit 1
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('reference/domain.py')
s = p.read_text()
old = 'if not 1 <= len(title) <= 120:'
assert s.count(old) == 1
p.write_text(s.replace(old, 'if not 0 <= len(title) <= 120:'))
PY
git add reference/domain.py
git commit -m 'Practice a validation defect for the CI gate'
git push -u origin practice/ci-empty-title
explain: Create a dedicated practice branch. The asserted single replacement allows an empty normalized title.
Commit and push only that defect. Open an MR targeting main in GitLab and inspect its required pipeline.
An explicit failure branch stops the sequence instead of letting later commands run after a failed prerequisite. Correct the cause and reopen Bash if the guard closed this terminal.
inject.expected: The existing blank-title test fails; the MR shows a failed pipeline and the configured merge restriction.
inject.troubleshoot: If no relevant test fails, inspect the test selection and exit handling. Do not add an unconditional failure to disguise a missing behavior assertion.

investigate.code:
git show --stat HEAD
git diff main...HEAD -- reference/domain.py
explain: show identifies the change in this commit. diff with three dots shows the feature change since its merge base with main.
investigate.expected: Exactly the intended lower-bound change, corresponding to the failing test.
investigate.troubleshoot: Compare the pipeline commit SHA to this local commit before diagnosing stale output.

hints: The test should protect the contract already taught in week 3.
Inspect whether any job uses allow_failure or ignores command exits.

explanation: Allowing length zero violates the task contract. Revert the deliberate commit and require the same MR pipeline to pass. Keep both runs as evidence that the gate detects a meaningful defect.

explain: The inverse commit preserves the failed change in history. push sends the repair to the same MR branch.
recover.expected: A new pipeline runs against the repaired commit.
recover.troubleshoot: If HEAD is no longer the deliberate defect, inspect the log and revert its actual hash.

explain: Record the defect/recovery history and a clean working tree. In GitLab verify the latest exact commit passes both jobs and the previously blocked MR is now eligible under the configured policy.
verification.expected: Two distinct runs: failing defect and passing repair, with the correct commit IDs.
verification.troubleshoot: A passing old pipeline is not evidence for the latest commit.

questions.prompt: What does a pending job tell you?
questions.answer: Usually only that GitLab has not assigned an eligible runner yet. Inspect runner availability, tags, executor and quota before changing application code.

questions.prompt: Why does artifacts:when:always not make tests optional?
questions.hint: Separate evidence retention from command status.
questions.answer: It retains evidence after failure. The script's nonzero exit still fails the job unless explicitly ignored or configured as allowed failure.

questions.prompt: Who can effectively use a job's credentials?
questions.answer: Anyone able to alter code executed in that credential-bearing job can attempt to use its authority. Masking output is not a substitute for controlling which changes run with secrets.

exercise.brief: Document and demonstrate the project's change gate with a failing and repaired MR.
constraints: Do not merge the deliberate defect or bypass protection to claim success.
deliverables: Pipeline links/commit IDs, failed assertion, repair and available merge-control settings.
acceptance: The meaningful defect fails and the repair passes.
You explain runner location and available authority.
Duplicate branch/MR behavior matches the workflow rules.
hints: Inspect pipeline source and commit SHA in GitLab.
solution: Create the MR, observe the red requirement, repair through a new commit and compare both runs.
Record any unavailable policy feature as a limitation with a named manual release-owner check.

explain: Return to main after closing or merging the repaired MR according to your review. Keep the branch history and pipeline evidence until the capstone.
cleanup.expected: A known local branch and no accidental uncommitted defect.
cleanup.troubleshoot: If the repaired MR was merged, git pull --ff-only updates main without creating an unexpected merge commit.
